record.paper_title: An open problem: Why are motif-avoidant attractors so rare in asynchronous Boolean networks?
record.original_question: Why are motif-avoidant attractors so rare under asynchronous update in Boolean networks, where a Boolean network is a discrete dynamical system whose variables are ON/OFF, asynchronous update changes one variable per time step, attractors are terminal recurrent state sets, minimal trap spaces are inescapable subspaces of the state space, and a motif-avoidant attractor is a complex attractor that lies outside every minimal trap space? The explanation should account for real-world biological Boolean networks, sparse and dense random Boolean networks, the role of input-node canalization, and why the observed hints do not yet yield a complete computational characterization of motif avoidance.

evidence.quote: An open problem: Why are motif-avoidant attractors so rare in asynchronous Boolean networks?

Despite recent efforts [21, 22], motif-avoidant attractors (MAAs) are still poorly understood, especially under asynchronous update. Empirical evidence suggests that motif-avoidant attractors are exceedingly rare in real-world biological networks [11, 23], but to the best of our knowledge, this observation has not been quantified before.
These hints do not yet give the whole picture, but they may point the way to a more complete understanding and computationally efficient characterization of motif avoidance.

artifact.status_search_result: The problem is explicitly posed as an open problem in a 2024/2025 contribution to the Journal of Mathematical Biology. Recent work (2025) provides large-scale empirical quantification of MAA rarity, shows MAAs are fragile to linear node extensions, and improves bounds on delays required to disrupt them, but does not provide a complete computational characterization of motif avoidance. Thus the problem remains open, with partial progress.
